title: Effect of elevated CO2 on crop yield in FACE experiments
research_question: Does elevated atmospheric CO2 increase crop yield in Free-Air CO2 Enrichment (FACE) and similar open-field experiments?

population.description: Annual crops grown in FACE (Free-Air CO2 Enrichment) experiments at elevated CO2 (~550-600 ppm) vs ambient CO2 (~370-400 ppm)

intervention.description: Elevated atmospheric CO2 concentration in FACE experiments (typically 550-600 ppm)

comparator.description: Ambient CO2 concentration (~400 ppm or concurrent ambient)
comparator.definition: Same crop grown at ambient atmospheric CO2 levels

primary.description: Crop grain yield or total aboveground biomass
primary.direction_of_interest: positive (elevated CO2 expected to increase C3 crop yield)

primary_outcomes: Crop grain yield or total aboveground biomass
typical_effect_size: +13% for C3 grain yield at ~550 ppm (FACE), +0% for C4 crops
important_moderators: Crop species (wheat, rice, soybean, maize, etc.)
Water availability (irrigated vs rainfed vs drought-stressed)
extraction_priorities: 1. CRITICAL: Extract yield for BOTH elevated CO2 AND ambient CO2 treatments
2. Control = ambient CO2; Treatment = elevated CO2
3. Extract EACH crop species separately if multiple tested
5. Record CO2 concentration level for both treatment and control
6. Record N and water treatments if co-manipulated
tc_confusion_warnings: Control is AMBIENT CO2, Treatment is ELEVATED CO2

FACE = Free-Air CO2 Enrichment — outdoor field plots with CO2 fumigation. Exclude OTC (open-top chambers), growth chambers, greenhouses. The elevated CO2 concentration should be ambient + ~200 ppm (550-600 ppm total).
FACE experiments typically have few true replicates (rings) — n may be 3-4
Some papers report multi-year results — extract each year separately
CO2 x temperature or CO2 x drought factorials: extract CO2 effect at each level of other factor
C4 crops (maize, sorghum, sugarcane) expected to show little/no CO2 response

search.seed_papers_description: Long et al. 2006 (Science 312:1918, FACE-specific cereal yield primary benchmark) and Ainsworth & Long 2021 (Global Change Biology, comprehensive FACE review secondary reference)

inclusion_criteria: Primary experiment comparing elevated vs ambient CO2 on crops
Reports yield or biomass data (numeric means)
Elevated CO2 is an experimental treatment (not natural gradient)
Includes both elevated and ambient CO2 groups
exclusion_criteria: No yield or biomass data (only photosynthesis, stomatal conductance, etc.)
Natural CO2 springs or volcanic vents (not controlled experiment)
Growth chamber or greenhouse CO2 enrichment — not FACE
Only reports growth/biomass without grain yield data

published_pooled_effect.notes: Long SP, Ainsworth EA, Leakey ADB, Nosberger J, Ort DR. Science 2006 Jun 30;312(5782):1918-21. PMID 16809532. Title: 'Food for Thought: Lower-Than-Expected Crop Yield Stimulation with Rising CO2 Concentrations'. Key finding: elevated CO2 enhanced yield in FACE experiments by ~50% less than in prior enclosure studies. C3 grain cereals (wheat, rice) in FACE: approximately +8% (commonly cited figure; paper reports enclosure estimates of ~15-17% for cereals, FACE approximately half that). C3 legumes (soybean): approximately +13% in FACE. This is a perspective/synthesis article, not a formal statistical meta-analysis; it does not report formal 95% CIs for the pooled FACE effect. The estimate field uses 8% as the FACE-specific cereal estimate (the primary benchmark-aligned target for this pipeline). For CI overlap evaluation (P2), the benchmark range is approximately +5% to +13% for FACE C3 cereals. Scope: FACE experiments only, C3 grain crops. Open access via PubMed PMID 16809532.

benchmark_secondary.notes: Ainsworth & Long 2021, GCB vol 27(1):27-49, PMID 33135850. Broader C3 crop estimate across all study types: ~+18% under non-stress conditions (k=186 independent studies, 14 FACE sites). Full text is closed access (Wiley GCB); exact 95% CI not obtainable from abstract. This estimate includes legumes and root crops (higher response) pooled with cereals (lower response). Kept as secondary reference; Long et al. 2006 is primary because it is FACE-specific, cereal-focused, and open-access.
